doc.title: Bobby Militello interviewed by Monk Rowe, Buffalo, New York, October 14, 2002

title: Keeping club audiences satisfied: good shows and the break-even formula
summary: Rowe asks how an owner addresses disappointed customers; Militello says he books good shows, posts sidemen and prices from a break-even seat formula.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Managers, bookers and the business of getting work

blocks.x: I was going to ask about that. I had an experience a couple of different times in New York where you go to like the Iridium, and by myself I think I spent $60, and I saw a band that had two very well known musicians on it but was obviously an unrehearsed, it was like a throw together gig you know. Which of course is typical. But I didn’t leave feeling great. Because I had to leave after the first set too or pay again. And so as an owner, how do you address my unhappiness?

Well number one is I usually put good shows together so I know that my shows that you’re going to get are going to be good shows. Some of the jazz shows you don’t know who the players are going to be when they come in but for the most part you can tell by knowing, which I know most of the cats so I know what they’re like and I know that they’ll come in with a good band and the whole bit. So as much as I can I get those details ahead of time and post them with everything — who the sidemen are in the band so everybody can know, which in a lot of circumstances, Lincoln Goines or any of the cats are in the band well that’s a selling point. So that’s the first thing we do is make sure we put good shows together, whatever kind of shows they are. The second thing is we make sure that the pricing of the show — I have a formula that I used and basically that formula basically breaks the room down into how many seats it has, how much money it costs me to promote the concert and whatever other extremities — back line rentals, etc, etc. Come up with a number. Take that number, take around 65 percent of the seats in the house. That should break me even. Sometimes 70, 75, it depends how much the band really costs you. If I really want — like when I did Pat Methany for three days we ran at 85 percent. That means 85 percent of those seats have to be filled or I’m going to lose money on the show. But what you do is you take that, you advertise the cost, you take a look and you see what that ticket price is. Now to make it even fairer you can take and say instead of one ticket price we’re going to go with advanced and day of show. If you wait until the day of show you pay more. If you buy them in advance you pay less. Object being that the spread allows me then to reduce the advance ticket price and that the people that buy day of show pay the freight because they prefer not to buy in advance and that’s cool, that’s fine. So by doing the spread on that level that allows me to drop one or two dollars off that advance ticket price. So basically this is what I mean by Buffalo real prices. Also, negotiating with agents and telling them, hold on guys, we’re in Buffalo, you’re not in New York, you’re not in Philly. Don’t hit me with the high ball national rate because you’re not going to get it in Buffalo and you’re not going to draw the number of people you think you are.
